nameStory: The Painted Lady gets her beautiful name from the artistic splashes of orange, black, and white that decorate her wings like delicate brushstrokes on canvas. Early naturalists thought these intricate patterns resembled the elaborate face paint and colorful dress of fashionable ladies from centuries past.
description: The Painted Lady is a medium-sized butterfly with a wingspan of about 2-3 inches, wearing a stunning coat of salmon-orange wings decorated with black spots and white patches. This remarkable traveler is actually the world's most widespread butterfly species, found on every continent except Antarctica and South America. In New England, you'll see them from late spring through fall, often in gardens where they love to sip nectar from flowers. They're part of the brush-footed butterfly family, meaning their front legs are reduced to tiny, brush-like appendages used for tasting.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive salmon-orange base color with bold black spots and white patches near the wingtips - the pattern looks like someone flicked white paint onto orange canvas

idTips.label: Wing Shape
idTips.description: Wings have a slightly scalloped or wavy outer edge, not smooth and rounded like some other butterflies

idTips.label: Underwing Markings
idTips.description: When wings are closed, the undersides show a beautiful marbled pattern of brown, gray, and cream with distinctive eye-spots that feel bumpy to gentle touch

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a robust, sturdy body about as thick as a pencil, and wings that span roughly the width of your palm

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with strong, purposeful wingbeats in a relatively straight line, not the erratic dancing flight of smaller butterflies

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen in open, sunny areas basking with wings spread wide, and tends to be less skittish than many other butterflies

habitat: Painted Ladies thrive in open, sunny areas throughout New England including gardens, fields, meadows, parks, and roadsides from sea level to mountain elevations. They're particularly drawn to areas with abundant flowers like thistles, asters, and garden plants such as buddleia and zinnias. You'll often spot them in disturbed habitats like vacant lots or along trail edges where weedy flowers bloom.

seasonality.spring: First arrivals appear in late spring (May-June) as migrants from the south, looking fresh and vibrant as they seek flowers and mating opportunities.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in summer when you'll see multiple generations, including worn adults with tattered wing edges and fresh offspring with pristine wing patterns.
seasonality.fall: Fall brings the most spectacular numbers as northern populations begin their southern migration, often gathering in large groups at flower patches to fuel up.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England winters - the species dies out locally and must recolonize each year from southern populations.

funFact: Painted Ladies are incredible long-distance migrants that can travel over 100 miles per day and up to 1,000 miles total, sometimes flying so high they've been spotted by radar crossing mountain ranges at altitudes where you'd need an oxygen mask to breathe!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with American Ladies, but Painted Ladies have four eye-spots on their underwings while American Ladies have just two large ones. Memory trick: 'Painted Ladies have more paint spots' - count the eye-spots on the underwing and you'll know for sure.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'ladies,' both male and female butterflies share similar coloring, unlike many butterfly species where males and females look quite different. The name 'Cosmopolitan' was once used in North America because of their worldwide distribution.
compareHints: Painted Ladies differ from American Ladies by having smaller, more numerous eye-spots on their underwings (four vs. two), and from Red Admirals by their overall orange coloration rather than the Red Admiral's black base with red bands. Painted Ladies also lack the distinctive white patches that Red Admirals display on their forewings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American Lady differs from Red Admiral by having orange (not red and black) wings and lacking the Red Admiral's distinctive white band across the forewings.
Unlike its Vanessa relatives, the Red Admiral has distinct red (not orange) markings arranged in clear bands rather than scattered patches.
